11940:
Parsimony means extreme and excessive unwillingness to spend money or use resources — going so far beyond careful budgeting that it becomes a fault.

Think of it this way: there's a spectrum of how people handle money.

Generous → Balanced → Careful → Frugal → Parsimonious

Parsimony sits at the far negative end. It's not just being careful or thrifty — it's being unreasonably tight with money or resources, even when spending would be perfectly justified or even necessary.
What Makes It Different from Just "Being Careful"

This is the most important thing to understand. The word carries a clear negative judgment. When you call someone's behavior parsimony, you're saying they've crossed a line — from sensible saving into something almost irrational or mean-spirited.

A person who skips a restaurant meal to save money is being frugal. But a person who refuses to buy medicine because it costs too much, or who lets guests go hungry rather than spend money on food, is showing parsimony.

The key signal is this: parsimony causes harm, discomfort, or embarrassment — either to the person themselves or to others — and yet the person still won't loosen their grip on resources.
It Doesn't Only Apply to Money

While money is the most common context, parsimony can apply to anything that someone gives out stingily — praise, time, kindness, effort, or words.

For example: a manager who never compliments their team, even when the work is excellent, can be said to show parsimony with praise. A government that barely funds its schools despite having the budget for it is showing parsimony in public spending.

Parsimony has a second, completely separate meaning used in science, philosophy, and logic — and here, it's not a negative word at all. In fact, it's a virtue.

In these fields, parsimony means the principle of choosing the simplest explanation that fits the facts, without adding unnecessary complexity.

This is also known as Occam's Razor — the idea that if two explanations both account for what you observe, you should prefer the simpler one. Scientists call this the principle of parsimony or scientific parsimony.

Example: You wake up and your sandwich is gone. Two explanations:

  • Your roommate ate it.
  • A stranger broke in, ate only the sandwich, stole nothing else, and left no trace.

The parsimonious explanation is the first one — it's the simplest that fits the evidence.

In this context, parsimony means economy of assumptions — don't multiply complexity beyond what's necessary to explain something.

Here are examples covering both meanings so you can see how the word behaves naturally in context:

Everyday/negative sense:

  • "The landlord's parsimony was legendary — he refused to fix the heating even in the middle of winter."
  • "Her parsimony meant she never tipped at restaurants, which embarrassed everyone she dined with."
  • "The company's parsimony with employee salaries led to its best workers quitting."

Scientific/philosophical sense:

  • "The theory was accepted partly due to its parsimony — it explained everything with just two simple assumptions."
  • "In biology, parsimony guides researchers to favor evolutionary trees with the fewest changes."

The word parsimony belongs to a small family:

  • Parsimony (noun) — the quality or behavior itself. "His parsimony was shocking."
  • Parsimonious (adjective) — describing a person or thing that shows parsimony. "She was parsimonious with compliments."
  • Parsimoniously (adverb) — describes how something is done in a parsimonious way. "The aid was parsimoniously distributed."

One last thing worth knowing: parsimony is a formal, slightly elevated word. You won't hear it in casual conversation every day. People in everyday speech usually say "cheapness," "stinginess," or "being tight-fisted." You're more likely to see parsimony in:

  • Formal writing or literary criticism
  • Academic or scientific papers
  • Journalism and commentary
  • Philosophy and logic

When you encounter it, you now know exactly what it means — and in which direction (negative criticism of excessive stinginess, or positive praise of elegant simplicity) the writer is pointing.
11941:
A part is a piece of something larger — something that, together with other pieces, makes up a whole. Think of a pizza: each slice is a part of the pizza. The pizza itself is the whole; the slices are its parts.

This one idea — a piece of a larger whole — runs through almost every meaning of "part." Keep this in mind as you read on.

1. A Piece or Portion of Something

The most common meaning. A part is a section, chunk, or portion of something — whether physical or not.

  • "She ate a part of the cake and saved the rest."
  • "A large part of his life was spent traveling."
  • "That part of the book is very confusing."

The "something" doesn't have to be a physical object. It can be an idea, a story, a period of time, or anything that can be divided.

2. A Component — A Piece That Makes a Machine or System Work

When something is built from many pieces that each serve a purpose — like a car, a computer, or an engine — each individual piece is called a part.

  • "The mechanic ordered a new part for the engine."
  • "Spare parts for this old phone are hard to find."
  • "One part of the machine broke, and the whole thing stopped working."

These parts are not just random pieces — each one has a specific job in making the whole thing function.

3. A Role in a Play, Film, or Performance

In theatre and film, a part is the character that an actor plays. It is exactly the same as a "role."

  • "She got the part of the queen in the school play."
  • "He auditioned for a part in the movie but wasn't selected."
  • "Playing the part of a villain is not easy."

The word "part" is used here because the character is literally a part of the larger story — one piece among many characters.

4. A Person's Voice or Instrument in Music

In music, a part is the specific set of notes assigned to one voice or one instrument in a piece of music. When many musicians play together, each person follows their own "part."

  • "The violin part in this symphony is very difficult."
  • "She sang the soprano part beautifully."
  • "Can you play the piano part while I sing?"

Again, each part is a piece of the larger musical whole.

5. A Section of a Book, Document, or Work

Long books, films, or courses are often divided into large sections. Each of these sections is called a part.

  • "The novel is divided into three parts."
  • "Part Two of the film is much more exciting than Part One."
  • "We finished Part 3 of the course today."

6. A Region or Area

"Part" (often used in the plural — "parts") can refer to a geographic region or area of the world, especially in a vague or general sense.

  • "What part of India are you from?"
  • "In these parts, it rains heavily every July." (= In this area/region)
  • "He's not from these parts." (= He's not from around here)

7. A Person's Involvement or Share in Something

A part can mean someone's involvement, role, or responsibility in an event or situation — how much they contributed to something, good or bad.

  • "She played no part in the decision." (= She was not involved)
  • "He accepted his part in causing the problem." (= His share of responsibility)
  • "Everyone must do their part." (= their individual contribution)

Notice the subtle difference from Meaning 3 (theatrical role): here, it's about real-life involvement, not performance.

8. One Side in a Dispute or Disagreement

A part can mean one side when people are disagreeing or debating. This is used in phrases like "take someone's part."

  • "She always took my part when others criticized me." (= She sided with me / defended me)
  • "It's difficult to take anyone's part in such a complicated argument."

9. A Line in the Hair

A part (sometimes called a parting) is the line on your head where your hair is divided and combed to either side.

  • "She has a middle part." (= her hair is divided down the centre)
  • "He switched from a side part to a middle part."
  • "The barber made a sharp part on the left side."

10. "Parts" (Plural) — Abilities or Talents

When used in the plural in a slightly formal or old-fashioned way, "parts" can mean a person's natural abilities, skills, or qualities.

  • "He is a man of many parts." (= He is a person with many different talents and abilities)
  • "A woman of considerable parts." (= A woman of great ability)

This usage is not common in everyday conversation today, but you will encounter it in books and literature.
Important Phrases Using "Part" as a Noun

These are very common expressions. You'll see them constantly.

"For the most part"
→ Meaning: mostly; in general; in most cases

  • "The film was, for the most part, very good."

"In part"
→ Meaning: partly; to some degree — not completely

  • "The delay was in part due to bad weather."

"For my part / for his part / for her part"
→ Meaning: as far as I am concerned; speaking for myself

  • "For my part, I think the plan is a good one."
  • "For her part, she was happy with the result."

"Take part (in something)"
→ Meaning: to participate; to be involved in something

  • "Everyone is encouraged to take part in the discussion."

"In good part"
→ Meaning: without taking offence; in a good-natured way

  • "He took the joke in good part." (= He was not upset by it)

"Part and parcel"
→ Meaning: an essential or inevitable part of something

  • "Long hours are part and parcel of the job."

"The better part of"
→ Meaning: most of; a large portion of

  • "We waited for the better part of an hour." (= almost a full hour; most of the hour)

"On the part of / on someone's part"
→ Meaning: done by someone; coming from someone's side

  • "There was a clear lack of effort on his part." (= He was clearly not making an effort)
  • "It was a mistake on the part of the management." (= The management made a mistake)

Even though "part" has many meanings, they all share one thread: something that belongs to, or comes out of, something larger.

| A machine has → parts (components) |
| A story has → parts (sections and characters/roles) |
| A piece of music has → parts (each instrument's share) |
| A person has → a part in events (their share of involvement) |
| The world is divided into → parts (regions) |
| Your hair is divided by → a part (a line of division) |

In every case, "part" points to something that is not the whole — it is always a piece of something bigger.

"Part" (noun) fundamentally means a piece of a larger whole. Depending on context, this "piece" can be:

  • a literal portion of an object
  • a component in a machine
  • an actor's role
  • a musician's assigned notes
  • a section of a book or film
  • a region of a place
  • someone's involvement in a situation
  • one side in a dispute
  • the line dividing your hair
  • (in plural) a person's talents

Master these, and you have a complete understanding of "part" as a noun.
11942:
To "part with" someone or something means to give up, let go of, or separate from someone or something — and it almost always suggests that doing so is difficult, sad, or unwanted.

The core idea is reluctance. You are not happily throwing something away. You are letting go of something (or someone) that means something to you, even if you have no choice.

Think of it this way: You part with something when letting it go costs you something emotionally.

The word "part" here is used as a verb, not a noun. It means to separate or to move away from. The word "with" connects the action to the object (the thing or person you are separating from).

So literally, you are separating yourself with (from) something. Over time, this became the fixed idiom "part with."

1. Parting with a Thing (Most Common Use)

This is when you give away, sell, hand over, or lose a possession — especially one you love or value.

Examples:

  • "She refused to part with her late mother's jewelry, no matter how much money she was offered."
  • "He finally had to part with his old guitar because he needed rent money."
  • "I've had this coat for 20 years. I just can't bring myself to part with it."
  • "The collector was not willing to part with even a single rare coin."

In everyday life, this use appears very often when people talk about money, possessions, memories, or anything they hold dear.

2. Parting with a Person (Less Common, But Correct)

This use refers to saying goodbye to someone or being separated from a person, again with a sense of sadness or difficulty.

Examples:

  • "It was heartbreaking to part with her best friend when she moved to another country."
  • "The children cried when they had to part with their grandfather at the airport."

A small but important note for learners: When talking about people, native speakers often prefer the phrase "part from" someone (e.g., "She parted from her friend at the gate"). "Part with" a person is grammatically fine and understood, but "part from" a person feels more natural in many contexts. When talking about things or possessions, however, "part with" is always the correct and natural choice — you would never say "part from my car."
The Emotional Weight: Why "Part With" Is Not Just "Give"

This is the most important thing to understand. Compare:

  • "She gave away her old dress." → Simple, neutral. No emotion implied.
  • "She parted with her old dress." → Implies the dress meant something to her. Letting it go was not easy.

The idiom carries hidden emotion. It signals that the person has an attachment to what they are giving up. This is why you will very often see words like reluctantly, finally, painfully, unwillingly, or phrases like couldn't bear to, had no choice but to, hated to placed near "part with" in sentences.

More examples showing this emotional layer:

  • "He reluctantly parted with his prized stamp collection."
  • "They finally parted with their family home after 40 years."
  • "I hated to part with the money, but the repairs were necessary."

The structure is simple and always the same:

Subject + part with + object (noun/pronoun)

SubjectVerb phraseObject
Shecouldn't part withher old diary.
Wehad to part withthe dog.
Herefused to part withhis savings.
  • It is always transitive — "part with" must always be followed by an object. You cannot say "She parted with" and stop there. The sentence needs to name what or who she parted with.
Common Phrases You'll Hear Around This Idiom

These are natural combinations that appear regularly in speech and writing:

  • "couldn't bear to part with" — couldn't emotionally handle giving it up
  • "reluctant/unwilling to part with" — not wanting to give it up
  • "forced to part with" — had no choice
  • "finally parted with" — did it eventually, after a long time or struggle
  • "hard/difficult to part with" — emotionally tough to let go
  • "willingly part with" — used often in the negative, as in "she wouldn't willingly part with a single penny"

These phrases carry a similar meaning to "part with":

  • "Let go of" — "I can't let go of this old photograph."
  • "Give up" — "He gave up his prized watch." (slightly more neutral)
  • "Relinquish" — formal word, same idea: "She relinquished her claim."
  • "Surrender" — often used in more formal or dramatic contexts
  • "Dispose of" — more neutral, less emotional

None of these fully capture the emotional reluctance that "part with" conveys as naturally and as powerfully.

"Part with" works comfortably in both formal and informal situations. You can use it in a novel, a business conversation, a newspaper article, or a casual chat with a friend. It is a versatile, timeless idiom.

FeatureDetail
Core meaningTo give up or separate from something/someone, usually reluctantly
Used mostly forPossessions, money, valued things
Also used forPeople (though "part from" is also common for people)
Key emotionReluctance, sadness, difficulty
GrammarSubject + part with + object (always needs an object)
RegisterBoth formal and informal

In one sentence: "Part with" means to let go of something or someone you care about — and the phrase almost always whispers that doing so hurts a little.
11943:
To partake means to take part in something or to have a share of something. Think of the word itself — it's almost hiding its own meaning: part + take. You take a part of something. You step into something and become a part of it.

It is a formal word. People rarely use it in casual, everyday speech. You'll mostly encounter it in formal writing, speeches, polite invitations, or older literature.

Meaning 1 — To participate or join in (partake in something)

When you partake in something, you actively join and take part in an activity, event, or experience.

Examples:

  • "Everyone was welcome to partake in the celebration."
  • "He refused to partake in the debate."
  • "Students are encouraged to partake in community service."

A simple test: if you can replace it with "take part in" or "participate in" and the sentence still makes sense, you're looking at this meaning.

Meaning 2 — To eat, drink, or consume (partake of something)

When you partake of food or drink, you consume some of it. This is a polite, old-fashioned way to say you eat or drink something.

Examples:

  • "Would you care to partake of some tea?"
  • "The guests partook of a lavish meal."
  • "She politely declined to partake of the wine."

A simple test: if you can replace it with "have some of" and the sentence still makes sense, you're looking at this meaning.

Meaning 3 — To have the qualities of something (partake of something — literary use)

Less commonly, partake of can mean that something shares the characteristics or qualities of something else. You'll mostly see this in formal essays or literary writing.

Examples:

  • "His art partakes of both classical and modern styles."
    (= His art has qualities of both classical and modern styles.)
  • "The atmosphere of the town partook of something almost magical."
    (= The atmosphere had a quality that was almost magical.)

The preposition you use changes the meaning:

  • Partake in → used for activities, events, experiences (participation)
  • Partake of → used for food, drink, or qualities (consumption or character)

Getting the preposition wrong sounds unnatural, so it's worth remembering this distinction.

Also important: partake almost always needs a preposition. You cannot just say "I partook the meal" — it needs to be "I partook of the meal."

Partake is an irregular verb, meaning it doesn't follow the usual "-ed" pattern in the past.

  • Base form: partake
  • He/she/it (present): partakes
  • Past simple: partook (not "partaked")
  • Past participle: partaken (used with "have/has/had")
  • -ing form: partaking

Examples across tenses:

  • "Will you partake in the ceremony?" (future)
  • "She partook of the dessert." (past simple)
  • "They have partaken in many such events before." (present perfect)
  • "He is partaking in the discussion." (present continuous)
Tone and when to use it

Partake is formal and slightly old-fashioned. In everyday casual speech, most people would say "join in," "take part in," "eat," or "drink" instead. Here's how the register shifts:

  • Casual → "Do you want some cake?"
  • Formal → "Would you like to partake of the cake?"
  • Casual → "Come join the game!"
  • Formal → "You are welcome to partake in the game."

Use partake when you want to sound polished, respectful, or deliberately literary. Using it in casual text messages or conversations would sound stiff and out of place.
How it compares to similar words

Partake in vs. Participate in:
These are very close in meaning — both mean to take part in something. The difference is mainly formality. "Participate" sits comfortably in both formal and informal settings. "Partake in" leans more formal and literary.

  • "Students participated in the science fair." (neutral)
  • "Students partook in the science fair." (more formal, slightly unusual in modern speech)

Partake of vs. Indulge in:
Both can describe consuming or enjoying something, but "indulge" carries a sense of giving in to a pleasure — sometimes implying mild excess or self-reward. "Partake of" is more neutral and dignified.

  • "She indulged in a slice of chocolate cake." (treating herself, a hint of guilty pleasure)
  • "She partook of a slice of chocolate cake." (simply ate some, no emotional coloring)

Partake of vs. Share:
"Share" focuses on dividing something among people. "Partake of" focuses on you personally taking or consuming your portion — it doesn't necessarily mean others are involved.

Partake inTo join and participate in an activity or event
Partake ofTo eat or drink something; or to have the qualities of something
FormalityFormal and old-fashioned
Past tensePartook
Past participlePartaken

In short: when you partake, you are stepping in and taking your share — whether that's a share of an experience, a meal, or even a quality.
11944: "Partial" has three distinct meanings in English. They look the same on paper but mean very different things depending on context. Once you understand all three, you'll never be confused by this word again.
Meaning 1 — Not complete; only a part of something

This is the most common meaning. When something is partial, it is not the whole thing. It is a piece, a portion, a fraction — but not all of it.

Think of it as the opposite of total, complete, or full.

Examples:

  • "The surgery was a partial success." → It succeeded in some ways, but not completely.
  • "She made a partial payment." → She paid some of the money, but not the full amount.
  • "There will be a partial solar eclipse tonight." → The moon will cover only part of the sun, not all of it.
  • "He has partial hearing loss." → He can still hear some things, but not everything.

The key question to ask yourself: Is the thing being described whole and complete, or is it only part of the way there? If it's only part of the way there, "partial" is being used in this sense.

Common words used nearby: partial loss, partial recovery, partial agreement, partial view, partial refund.
Meaning 2 — Biased; unfairly favoring one side

When a person is described as partial, it means they are not neutral. They have secretly taken a side. They favor one person, group, or idea over another — and this is considered unfair, especially when they are supposed to be neutral.

This meaning is the opposite of "impartial." An impartial person treats all sides equally and judges fairly. A partial person does not.

Examples:

  • "The referee was partial toward the home team." → The referee secretly favored the home team and made unfair calls.
  • "The committee's decision seemed partial." → Their decision appeared biased, not neutral.
  • "A judge must never be partial." → A judge must never secretly favor one side in a case.

The key question: Is this person supposed to be neutral and fair, but clearly isn't? If yes, "partial" is being used in this sense.

This meaning appears most often in formal, legal, professional, or official situations — anywhere fairness and neutrality are expected.
Meaning 3 — Having a particular fondness or liking for something

This meaning is softer and more personal. When you say you are partial to something, you mean you especially like it or have a personal preference for it. It's not about bias or unfairness — it's simply about taste or fondness.

Notice: This meaning almost always comes with the word "to" right after it. So watch for the pattern: partial to [something].

Examples:

  • "I'm quite partial to dark chocolate." → I personally love dark chocolate; it's a weakness of mine.
  • "He's always been partial to jazz music." → He has a special fondness for jazz.
  • "She's a little partial to staying up late." → She has a soft spot for staying up late.

The key question: Is someone expressing a personal liking or fondness? And is the word "to" nearby? If yes, this is the meaning.

At the heart of all three meanings is a single idea: not equal on all sides.

  • In Meaning 1, something is not equally distributed — you only have part of it, not all.
  • In Meaning 2, a person does not treat all sides equally — they lean toward one side unfairly.
  • In Meaning 3, a person does not like all things equally — they lean toward one thing in particular with fondness.

So "partial" always describes an imbalance of some kind — whether it's about completeness, fairness, or personal taste.
How to tell which meaning is being used

Context is everything. Ask yourself three quick questions:

  1. Is it describing how complete something is? → Meaning 1 (partial success, partial payment)
  2. Is it describing a person in a situation where fairness is expected? → Meaning 2 (a partial judge, a partial decision)
  3. Is it followed by "to" and describing a personal preference? → Meaning 3 (partial to coffee, partial to long walks)

The prefix "im-" means not. So impartial simply means not partial — meaning fair, neutral, and unbiased. This is the direct opposite of Meaning 2 above.

You'll often see impartial praised as a good quality: "We need an impartial investigation." And you'll sometimes see partial used as a criticism: "The jury was partial."

Understanding this pair — partial and impartial — will sharpen your sense of both words considerably.
11945: "Partiality" has two distinct but related meanings. Understanding both — and how they connect — will give you a complete picture of the word.

This is the most common and serious meaning. When someone shows partiality, they are treating one person, group, or side more favorably than others — not because that party deserves it, but because of personal feelings, relationships, or prejudice.

Think of a judge who secretly favors one side in a court case, or a teacher who gives better grades to students they personally like, regardless of the quality of their work. That judge and that teacher are both displaying partiality. The problem isn't just that they have a preference — the problem is that their role demands fairness, and they are failing to provide it.

This is why partiality in this sense carries a negative, even accusatory weight. It implies a compromise of integrity. When a referee consistently ignores fouls by one team but penalizes the other heavily, spectators will rightly say there is partiality in the officiating.

The direct opposite of partiality in this sense is impartiality — the quality of treating all sides equally and without favoritism. Judges, journalists, arbitrators, and umpires are all expected to act with impartiality.

Synonyms for this sense: bias, favoritism, prejudice, one-sidedness.
Meaning 2: A special fondness or preference for something

This second meaning is gentler and personal. Here, "partiality" simply means a particular liking or fondness for something — a preference that goes a little beyond ordinary enjoyment. There is nothing unfair or wrong about it; it is just a personal taste.

For example:

  • "She has a partiality for old black-and-white films." → She particularly loves them.
  • "He has always had a partiality for strong coffee." → It's his special preference.
  • "I confess a partiality toward detective novels." → I have a fondness for them above other genres.

Notice that in these sentences, "partiality" is followed by "for" or "toward" — a reliable signal that meaning 2 is in play.

Synonyms for this sense: fondness, liking, preference, weakness for, soft spot for, predilection.
How the two meanings are connected

Both meanings grow from the same core idea: leaning toward one side rather than treating everything equally. In meaning 1, this unequal leaning is a moral or professional failure — it is unfair. In meaning 2, the same leaning is perfectly acceptable — it is simply personal taste. The difference is context. No one is harmed by your partiality for jazz music. But a great deal can go wrong when a judge shows partiality toward a defendant.
How to tell which meaning is intended

Context almost always makes it clear:

  • Professional or ethical contexts — a judge, referee, journalist, teacher, official, examiner, or anyone whose job requires fairness → meaning 1 (unjust favoritism).
  • Personal preferences — food, music, books, places, hobbies — → meaning 2 (fondness).

A useful test: if the partiality harms someone else or violates a duty, it's meaning 1. If it's simply about what someone privately enjoys, it's meaning 2.

"Partiality" is a formal word. In everyday speech, people tend to say "bias" or "favoritism" for meaning 1, and "soft spot for" or "weakness for" something for meaning 2. You are more likely to encounter "partiality" in writing — in legal documents, editorials, academic texts, or formal speeches. When you do see it, it has a precise, slightly elevated quality that words like "bias" or "fondness" don't always carry.

"Partialities" (plural) is used but rare. You might see it when listing specific biases or specific fondnesses: "His partialities were well-known — he favored the aristocracy over commoners in almost every ruling."

What it describesUnfair favoring of one party over anotherA personal fondness or strong preference
ToneNegative — implies a failure of fairnessNeutral or warm — just a personal taste
Typical contextLaw, sports, journalism, grading, any role requiring fairnessFood, hobbies, art, lifestyle preferences

11946:
To participate means to take active part in something — to be involved in an activity, event, process, or situation in a way where you are actually doing something, not just watching or being present.

It's the difference between being in a room where a discussion is happening and actually speaking, listening, and contributing to that discussion. Both people are present; only one is participating.
The Key Idea: Active Involvement

The heart of this word is active engagement. When you participate, you are not a passive observer — you are a contributor. That contribution can take many forms:

  • Speaking up in a meeting
  • Casting a vote in an election
  • Running in a race
  • Answering questions in a class
  • Filling out a survey

In every case, you are doing something as part of a larger activity that involves others.
Who (or What) Can Participate

While people most commonly participate, the word extends to organizations, countries, groups, and institutions as well.

  • Students participate in discussions.
  • Companies participate in trade fairs.
  • Nations participate in peace negotiations.
  • Teams participate in tournaments.

Any entity capable of taking action can participate.
How to Use It Grammatically

The essential rule: "Participate" is always followed by the preposition "in" when an activity is mentioned.

  • ✅ She participated in the debate.
  • ✅ They refused to participate in the ceremony.
  • ❌ She participated the debate. (wrong — you cannot skip the preposition)

One common exception: when referring to committees, panels, or teams, "on" is also acceptable:

  • He was invited to participate on the expert panel.

"Participate" is an intransitive verb, which means it does not take a direct object on its own. You cannot "participate something" — you always participate in something or on something.
Degrees of Participation

Participation is not all-or-nothing. It exists on a spectrum:

  • Active / full participation — you are deeply involved, contributing significantly.
  • Minimal participation — you are technically involved but barely doing anything.

This is why you often see words like "actively," "fully," or "meaningfully" placed before it:

  • She actively participated in every session.
  • He barely participated in the group project.
Register: Formal or Informal?

"Participate" is slightly formal. It's the word you'd naturally find in academic papers, official documents, news reports, and professional settings.

In casual, everyday speech, people more often say:

  • "take part in" — the most common informal equivalent
  • "join in" — used especially for spontaneous or social activities

So while "She participated in the contest" and "She took part in the contest" mean the same thing, the first sounds more formal. Both are perfectly correct.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Understanding "participate" becomes sharper when you compare it with words that seem similar but aren't identical.

Attend — means to be physically present somewhere. You can attend a lecture without saying a word. But to participate in a lecture means you're engaging with it — asking questions, doing activities, responding to the teacher. Attending is possible without participating; participating usually requires some form of attendance.

Join — means to become a member of something or to enter and become part of a group. It emphasizes the act of entry. Participate emphasizes what you do once you are part of something.

  • She joined the club. (She became a member.)
  • She participated in the club's activities. (She was actively involved in what the club did.)

Contribute — means to give something specific — money, ideas, effort. It's often a part of participation. When you participate, you may contribute, but contribution is just one aspect of the broader action of participating.

Engage — similar to participate, but with a stronger emphasis on mental and emotional involvement. You can participate in a task mechanically; to engage suggests your mind and attention are genuinely invested.

Involve — usually used in the passive form ("be involved in") and is more about connection or association with something. Participation is more voluntary and active.
Common Collocations (Words That Naturally Go With "Participate")

These are the phrases you'll encounter most often:

  • participate in a meeting / discussion / debate
  • participate in a competition / contest / race
  • participate in an election / vote
  • participate in a study / research / survey / trial
  • participate in decision-making
  • participate in the process
  • actively / fully / voluntarily / directly participate
  • refuse / decline / be invited / be encouraged to participate
  • eligible to participate (meaning: allowed or qualified to take part)
Real-Life Examples Across Different Situations

Education:
Students who participate in classroom discussions tend to understand the material better than those who only listen.

Work:
All employees are expected to participate in the annual performance review process.

Politics:
When citizens participate in elections, they exercise their democratic right to influence who governs them.

Sports:
Despite an injury, he was determined to participate in the championship.

Research:
Over 500 volunteers participated in the clinical trial to test the new vaccine.

Social life:
She was nervous at first, but once she started participating in the group activities, she made friends quickly.

Online / digital:
You can participate in the live Q&A session by typing your questions in the chat.
A Common Mistake to Avoid

Many learners write or say "participate to" — this is incorrect.

  • ❌ He wants to participate to the event.
  • ✅ He wants to participate in the event.

Always use "in" (or occasionally "on" for panels/committees). Never "to," "at," or "for."
Summary in One Sentence

To participate means to be an active contributor to something — an event, a process, an activity, or a discussion — rather than merely watching or being present, and it is always used with the preposition "in."
11947:
A participle is a verb that has been modified so it can do the job of an adjective — that is, it describes or modifies a noun. At the same time, it still looks like a verb and retains some verb-like qualities. Think of it as a verb wearing an adjective's hat.

For example, take the verb burn. From it, you can get the participle burning, which can describe a noun: "a burning building." The word burning came from a verb, but here it is describing the noun building — just like any adjective would.

There are two kinds of participles in English:

1. The Present Participle

This is formed by adding -ing to the base verb.

  • run → running
  • laugh → laughing
  • build → building
  • cry → crying

It generally refers to an action that is active and ongoing.

2. The Past Participle

This is a little trickier because it has two forms depending on whether the verb is regular or irregular.

For regular verbs, it is formed by adding -ed or -d to the base verb:

  • burn → burned (or burnt)
  • close → closed
  • walk → walked

For irregular verbs, the past participle has its own unique form that you simply have to learn:

  • break → broken
  • eat → eaten
  • write → written
  • go → gone
  • sleep → slept

The past participle generally refers to an action that is completed or received (i.e., something done to the noun).

Participles serve three main roles in English.

Role 1: Acting as a Plain Adjective

This is the most straightforward use. The participle sits before (or sometimes after) a noun and directly describes it, just like any ordinary adjective.

Present participle examples:

  • "a running engine" (the engine is running — active, ongoing)
  • "a crying baby"
  • "the rising sun"

Past participle examples:

  • "a broken promise" (the promise has been broken — completed, done to it)
  • "a written agreement"
  • "the locked door"

Notice how broken, written, and locked all describe what has happened to the noun — the promise was broken, the agreement was written, the door was locked. This is the passive, completed quality of the past participle.

Role 2: Forming Verb Tenses (with helping verbs)

This is perhaps the most common way you encounter participles, even if you never realized they were participles. When combined with helping verbs (also called auxiliary verbs like be, have, will), participles form the different tenses of English.

The present participle + a form of "be" → forms continuous (or progressive) tenses:

  • "She is running." (present continuous)
  • "They were laughing." (past continuous)
  • "He will be sleeping." (future continuous)

Here, running, laughing, and sleeping are present participles working inside verb phrases.

The past participle + a form of "have" → forms perfect tenses:

  • "She has eaten." (present perfect)
  • "They had gone." (past perfect)
  • "He will have finished." (future perfect)

The past participle + a form of "be" → forms passive voice:

  • "The window was broken." (past passive)
  • "The letter has been written." (present perfect passive)

In all of these, the participle is doing the heavy lifting of expressing what kind of action or state is being described, while the helping verb carries the information about time and person.

Role 3: Leading a Participial Phrase

A participial phrase is a group of words that begins with a participle and together modifies a noun. It behaves like an expanded adjective.

Present participial phrase:

"Running down the street, the boy tripped over a stone."

Here, Running down the street is a participial phrase. The whole phrase describes the boy — it tells us what he was doing at the moment. The participle running is at the head of the phrase.

Past participial phrase:

"Exhausted by the long journey, she fell asleep immediately."

Here, Exhausted by the long journey describes she — it tells us her condition. Exhausted is the past participle heading this phrase.

Participial phrases are flexible. They can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence:

  • Beginning: "Broken beyond repair, the watch was thrown away."
  • Middle: "The watch, broken beyond repair, was thrown away."
  • End: "He threw away the watch, broken beyond repair."

There is a third, less commonly discussed form called the perfect participle. It is formed with "having" + past participle and expresses an action that was completed before another action happened.

  • "Having eaten dinner, she went for a walk." (She finished eating first, then walked.)
  • "Having studied all night, he felt confident in the exam."

This is useful when you want to emphasize the sequence of events — that one thing was fully done before the next thing began.
An Important Distinction: Participle vs. Gerund

You may wonder: "If the present participle ends in -ing, and gerunds also end in -ing, how are they different?"

The answer is: it depends on the job the word is doing in the sentence.

  • When an -ing word describes a noun (adjective role) or is part of a verb tense → it is a participle.
  • When an -ing word acts as a noun itself (the subject, object, etc.) → it is a gerund.

Compare:

  • "Swimming is good exercise." → Swimming is the subject of the sentence (it's a noun). This is a gerund.
  • "The swimming fish darted away." → Swimming describes fish (adjective role). This is a participle.
  • "She is swimming." → Swimming is part of the verb phrase (with the helping verb is). This is a participle.

Same -ing ending, different grammatical role — that is the only distinction.
A Common Error: The Dangling Participle

Because a participle or participial phrase modifies a noun, it must clearly point to the correct noun in the sentence. When it doesn't, it is called a dangling participle — and it often produces unintentionally funny or confusing sentences.

Dangling (wrong):

"Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful."

Who was walking — the person or the trees? Grammatically, the phrase walking down the street is closest to the trees, which makes it sound like the trees were walking. This is the error.

Corrected:

"Walking down the street, I found the trees beautiful."

Now walking clearly refers to I, which makes logical sense.

Another example:

Dangling (wrong):

"Exhausted and hungry, the pizza tasted amazing."

The pizza was exhausted and hungry? No — the person was. The participle has no proper noun to attach to.

Corrected:

"Exhausted and hungry, she found the pizza tasted amazing."

The rule is simple: the noun that the participial phrase modifies must be the subject of the main clause and must appear right at the start of that clause (or immediately after the phrase).

What it isA verb form used as an adjective (or in a verb phrase)
Present participleverb + -ing → running, eating, broken
Past participleverb + -ed or irregular form → walked, broken, eaten
Perfect participlehaving + past participle → having eaten, having gone
Jobs it doesAdjective before a noun; part of a verb tense; head of a participial phrase
Key errorDangling participle — phrase not clearly attached to the right noun

In short: a participle is where verbs and adjectives meet. It takes the energy and meaning of a verb but uses that energy to describe rather than to state. Once you start noticing participles, you will find them everywhere — in nearly every sentence you read or write.
11948:
A particle is an extremely small piece or portion of something — so small that it's often difficult or impossible to see with the naked eye. Think of it as the tiniest meaningful unit or fragment of a substance.

The word works across many different contexts, and depending on where you encounter it, it can mean slightly different things.

In ordinary language, a particle is simply a tiny fragment or piece of matter. When you see dust floating in a beam of sunlight, each of those tiny specks is a particle of dust. When you crush a cracker, the crumbs and the even tinier powder left behind are particles of cracker.

The key qualities in this sense:

  • It is small — usually too small to pick up individually with your fingers.
  • It is solid in nature (or at least a discrete, countable piece of something).
  • It is a fragment of a larger whole.

Examples in everyday use:

  • "There were particles of sand in my shoe."
  • "The air in that old house was full of dust particles."
  • "She found particles of glass on the floor after the vase broke."

This is where the word becomes especially important. In science, particle refers to a discrete unit of matter or energy, usually at a microscopic or subatomic scale.

There are a few levels here, from larger to smaller:

Macroscopic particles

These are particles you could in theory see under a microscope — like a particle of pollen, a particle of smoke, or a particle of soil. These are still tiny, but they are made up of many, many atoms.

Atomic and subatomic particles

As you go smaller, you reach the level of atoms — and then inside atoms. Here, "particle" refers to the fundamental building blocks of matter:

  • Protons — positively charged particles found in the nucleus (center) of an atom.
  • Neutrons — particles with no charge, also found in the nucleus.
  • Electrons — negatively charged particles that move around the nucleus.

These are called subatomic particles because they exist below (sub-) the level of the atom.

Go even smaller, and you get to elementary particles — the most basic, indivisible units of matter and energy that we currently know of. These include things like quarks (which make up protons and neutrons), photons (particles of light), and others studied in a branch of physics called particle physics.

The important idea in science is that particles are not just small pieces — they follow their own rules of behavior. How particles interact with each other determines virtually everything about how the physical world works: why things have mass, why light travels, why atoms bond together to form molecules.

Alpha and Beta particles (in nuclear physics)

You might also encounter these specific terms:

  • An alpha particle is a cluster of 2 protons and 2 neutrons released by a radioactive nucleus — essentially the same thing as a helium nucleus.
  • A beta particle is a fast-moving electron (or its antiparticle) released during radioactive decay.

These aren't new kinds of things — they're just specific particles that come up in the context of radioactivity.

In the study of language, particle has a completely different meaning. Here, it refers to a small, function word that doesn't neatly fit into the main grammatical categories (like noun, verb, adjective, or adverb) and that typically contributes meaning to a phrase rather than standing alone.

Different grammar traditions use "particle" somewhat differently, but here are the most common uses:

Phrasal verb particles

In English, words like up, down, out, off, in, away often combine with a verb to create a new meaning. In these combinations, the word following the verb is called a particle:

  • "She gave up." — Here, "up" is a particle. Notice that "give up" (to quit) means something entirely different from just "give."
  • "He turned down the offer." — "Down" is a particle.
  • "They ran out of time." — "Out" is a particle.

What makes it a particle (rather than a simple adverb or preposition) is that it's fused in meaning with the verb — the combination is an idiomatic unit.

The infinitive marker "to"

Some grammarians also call the word "to" in phrases like "to run" or "to think" a particle — because it marks the infinitive form of a verb but isn't quite a preposition in this role.

Negative and discourse particles

Words like "not," "well," "oh," "just" are sometimes called particles because they perform specific grammatical or conversational functions without fitting cleanly into other categories.

"Particle" is also used figuratively — often in negative constructions — to emphasize the complete absence of something:

  • "There was not a particle of truth in what he said." (= not even the tiniest bit of truth)
  • "She showed not a particle of remorse." (= absolutely no remorse)

In this usage, "particle" functions as an intensifier to stress totality — it's a literary or somewhat formal way of saying "not even the smallest amount."

Even across these different contexts — everyday life, physics, grammar, and figurative speech — the thread connecting them all is the same idea: something minimal, elemental, or smallest of its kind.

  • In physics, a particle is the smallest unit of matter.
  • In everyday language, it's an extremely small piece of a substance.
  • In grammar, it's a minimal word that contributes function rather than full meaning.
  • In figurative speech, it represents the smallest imaginable quantity of something.

ContextWhat "particle" means

In everyday life: A tiny fragment or piece of a substance — dust, sand, glass, pollen, etc.

In physics/science: A discrete unit of matter or energy — from visible specks all the way down to subatomic building blocks like protons, electrons, quarks, and photons. The scientific study of these is called particle physics.

In grammar: A small function word — like "up" in "give up," or "not" — that plays a grammatical role but doesn't fit cleanly into standard word categories.

In figurative language: Used in negative phrases to mean "not even the tiniest bit" of something.

The unifying idea across all uses: a particle is always elemental, minimal, and small — whether you're talking about matter, meaning, or metaphor.
11949: "Particular" has three distinct meanings, but they all share one underlying thread: singling something out from the general crowd. Once you feel that thread, the word clicks into place permanently.
Meaning 1 — One specific thing, not just any

This is the most common meaning. You use "particular" to point at one specific thing from a larger group — to say "I don't mean things in general, I mean this one."

Examples:

  • "I'm looking for a particular book." → Not just any book — one specific book I already have in mind.
  • "On this particular day, everything went wrong." → Not every day; this one specific day.
  • "Is there a particular reason you're asking?" → Do you have one specific reason, or are you asking casually?

The feeling: You are narrowing down from many to one. You are singling out one item from the whole crowd.

Compare the difference:

  • "I want a job." → Any job will do.
  • "I want a particular job." → There's a specific one I have in mind.

The second sentence quietly tells the listener: there's one I've already identified — not just anything.

Here, "particular" signals that something stands above the ordinary — it is more important, more intense, or more noteworthy than usual.

Examples:

  • "Pay particular attention to Chapter 3." → More attention than you'd normally give; Chapter 3 is especially important.
  • "She has a particular talent for music." → Not a run-of-the-mill talent — a remarkable, standout one.
  • "This is a matter of particular concern." → Not everyday concern — it deserves extra weight.
  • "He took particular care while handling the glass." → He was more careful than he would normally be.

The feeling: Whatever is described is not ordinary. It rises above the general level and demands special notice.

Notice how Meanings 1 and 2 are related but different:

  • Meaning 1 is about which one (this specific one, not others).
  • Meaning 2 is about how much (more than usual, not ordinary).

Both involve singling something out — one from a group, the other from the ordinary level.
Meaning 3 — Having very high, specific standards; not easily satisfied

When "particular" describes a person's attitude toward something, it means that person has precise standards, notices details carefully, and won't be happy unless things are just right. They are choosy, but in a deliberate, standards-driven way.

Examples:

  • "She is very particular about her coffee." → The temperature, the strength, the brand all matter to her. She won't accept just anything.
  • "My editor is particular about grammar." → He has high standards and will notice even small errors.
  • "He's not very particular about food." → He doesn't have strong preferences; he'll eat almost anything.
  • "She's particular about how her desk is arranged." → Things must be in the right place; small details matter to her.

The feeling: This person doesn't accept the general or the approximate. They have specific requirements and care about getting them met exactly.

"Particular" vs. "fussy": Both describe someone with high standards, but "particular" sounds more neutral or even respectable — it suggests careful, considered standards. "Fussy" can sound more negative or childish. Saying someone is particular often implies they know what they want and why.

This is one of the most common phrases built from this word, and it means "especially" or "specifically" — it highlights one item from a group as standing out above the rest.

Examples:

  • "I love all fruits, but mangoes in particular." → Among all fruits, mangoes especially.
  • "Is there anything in particular you'd like to discuss?" → Is there one specific thing on your mind, or just general talk?
  • "Nothing in particular." → Nothing specific; nothing that stands out.

Think of "in particular" as a spotlight: you've mentioned a group, and now you're shining the light on one member of that group.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

The grammar and context tell you:

Meaning 1 (specific): "Particular" appears before a noun, pointing at one thing.

"a particular street," "this particular issue," "that particular evening"

Meaning 2 (special/extra): "Particular" intensifies something — often paired with nouns like attention, care, interest, concern, importance.

"particular attention," "of particular importance," "with particular care"

Meaning 3 (choosy/high standards): "Particular" describes a person's attitude, often followed by about.

"particular about cleanliness," "very particular," "not at all particular about it"
The Core Idea — The Thread Connecting All Three Meanings

All three meanings are really one idea seen from different angles:

What is being singled out
Meaning 1Which one — this specific thing, not others
Meaning 2How much — this deserves more attention than the ordinary
Meaning 3The details — this person notices and cares about specifics

In plain words: Meaning 1 singles out which item. Meaning 2 signals that something rises above the ordinary level. Meaning 3 describes someone who won't settle for the general or approximate.

When you use or read the word "particular," ask yourself: Is something being singled out? What is it — a specific item, an intensity, or a standard? The answer will always point you to the right meaning.
A Few More Natural Examples Across All Three Meanings

• "I have no particular preference." → No specific preference; anything works. (Meaning 1)
  • "The project requires particular skill." → More than ordinary skill is needed. (Meaning 2)
  • "She's very particular about punctuality." → She has high standards; being even slightly late is not acceptable to her. (Meaning 3)
  • "Nothing in this report is of particular interest." → Nothing stands out as especially notable. (Meaning 2)
  • "Do you have a particular doctor in mind?" → Is there one specific doctor you're thinking of? (Meaning 1)
  • "He's not at all particular about how the room looks." → He has no strong standards about it; he doesn't mind. (Meaning 3)

That's everything you need. The word "particular" always carries the idea of singling something out — whether it's a specific item, an elevated level of importance, or a person's careful, detail-driven standards. Keep that core feeling in mind, and you'll read and use this word with full confidence in any context.
